clinical_knowledge.topic: Invasive cervical carcinoma, locally advanced evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Invasive cervical carcinoma, locally advanced is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Refer immediately to Gynecologic Oncology, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: postcoital bleeding, foul-smelling watery vaginal discharge, and visible friable cervical lesion confirming cervical cancer

Key HPI features: 45F presents with 6-month history of spotting after sexual intercourse (postcoital bleeding), intermenstrual bleeding, and a persistent, foul-smelling, pink-to-watery vaginal discharge. Has not had a Pap smear or gynecological exam in 12 years. Complains of recent mild deep pelvic aching and pain radiating down her right leg.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 84, BP 130/82. Speculum examination reveals a 3.5 cm exophytic, cauliflower-like, ulcerated, friable mass replacing the anterior cervical lip that bleeds profusely upon contact with a cotton swab. Bimanual and rectovaginal examination under anesthesia demonstrates nodular tumor induration extending into the upper two-thirds of the vagina and laterally into the right parametrium up to but not fixed to the pelvic sidewall. Cervical punch biopsies confirm High-Grade Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the cervix (positive for High-Risk HPV type 16). Pelvic MRI and PET-CT confirm a 3.8 cm cervical tumor with parametrial invasion and two enlarged right external iliac lymph nodes (1.4 cm, hypermetabolic).
Relevant background/PMH: No regular medical care for 12 years, 20 pack-year smoking history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Invasive cervical carcinoma, locally advanced.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cervicitis/cervical infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Postcoital bleeding.
management_principles: Because the tumor extends into the parametrium and involves pelvic lymph nodes (FIGO Stage IIIC1 / > IB3), patient is NOT a candidate for primary surgical radical hysterectomy

Curative-intent treatment consists of Primary Definitive Chemoradiation Therapy: External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT) to pelvis combined with concurrent weekly cisplatin chemotherapy (radiosensitizer), followed by intracavitary brachytherapy boost to the cervical mass
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 45F unscreened smoker presenting with classic symptoms of invasive cervical malignancy: postcoital bleeding, malodorous leukorrhea, and pelvic pain.

Speculum examination reveals a 3.5 cm exophytic, cauliflower-like, ulcerated, friable mass replacing the anterior cervical lip that bleeds profusely upon contact with a cotton swab. reference_soap.assessment: Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Cervix, FIGO Stage IIIC1 (T2b N1 M0 - parametrial and pelvic lymph node involvement).
reference_soap.plan: Refer immediately to Gynecologic Oncology. Because the tumor extends into the parametrium and involves pelvic lymph nodes (FIGO Stage IIIC1 / > IB3), patient is NOT a candidate for primary surgical radical hysterectomy. Curative-intent treatment consists of Primary Definitive Chemoradiation Therapy: External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT) to pelvis combined with concurrent weekly cisplatin chemotherapy (radiosensitizer), followed by intracavitary brachytherapy boost to the cervical mass.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical hallmarks of invasive cervical carcinoma (postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, malodorous watery discharge, friable cervical mass)
Understand the role of human papillomavirus (specifically high-risk oncogenic genotypes HPV 16 and 18) in cervical carcinogenesis and the importance of routine cytology screening
Perform and interpret clinical FIGO staging parameters (specifically evaluating vaginal and parametrial extension on bimanual/rectovaginal exam)

Differentiate indications for primary surgery (Radical Hysterectomy for early Stage IA-IB2) vs primary Chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin plus EBRT and brachytherapy for locally advanced Stage IB3-IVA with parametrial or node involvement)

teaching.one_liner: 45F with 6 months of postcoital bleeding, foul discharge, and no Pap smear in 12 years — found to have a friable cervical lesion.

must_ask.say: Does the bleeding happen specifically after intercourse?
Can you describe the discharge — color, smell, consistency?
When was your last Pap smear or pelvic exam?

must_ask.objective: Screen for leg pain/swelling (nodal or nerve involvement)
must_ask.say: Have you had any pain or swelling going down your leg?
Do you currently smoke, and how much?

history.answer: I have been noticing blood after having intercourse for the past six months, and recently I've also had this bad-smelling watery discharge.
My menstrual periods used to be every twenty-eight days like clockwork, but over the last several months the timing has become irregular with spotting in between.
My normal menstrual flow uses about three or four pads a day without large blood clots, which has not changed much.
My period bleeding usually lasts about five days, but now I often have lingering light spotting.
No, I have not missed or skipped periods for months at a time.
It started about six months ago as light red blood on the sheets and toilet paper right after intercourse, and lately I also spot randomly between my periods.
history.topic: Bleeding after sex and between periods

history.answer: It is a thin, pink-to-watery discharge that runs almost constantly, and it has an unpleasant, rotten odor that does not wash off.
For the past few weeks, I have felt a continuous dull ache deep in my lower pelvis that sometimes aches down into my right leg.
I don't have painful urination or blood in my stool, though I feel mild pelvic pressure when my bladder is full.
I have felt more worn out and tired after my shifts at work, but I haven't had severe lightheadedness, shortness of breath, or heart palpitations.
No, I haven't had any unusual acne breakouts, excessive facial or body hair, or unexplained weight gain.
No, I don't feel unusually sensitive to warm or cold rooms, and my heart doesn't race.
No, I have never had milk or fluid leaking from my breasts, and I have not had headaches or trouble with my eyesight.
My weight has stayed around the same, and I haven't been dieting or doing strenuous exercise, though working on my feet is stressful.
No, I don't get nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or easy bruises, and I never bled excessively after dental work or cuts.
No, I am not taking birth control pills, hormone therapy, blood thinners, or any psychiatric medications, and I have never had an IUD.
I am sexually active with my long-term male partner, and we use condoms occasionally, but not every time.
I gave birth to two children vaginally in my twenties without complications, and I am not planning or trying to get pregnant.
I sometimes feel a little warm at night, but I have not had true drenching hot flashes or night sweats.
To be honest, I haven't had a Pap smear or a pelvic examination in twelve years because I didn't have insurance and kept putting it off.
I don't have diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of skipped periods, and my weight has been steady.
At first, I thought this was just a stubborn vaginal infection or irregular spotting because I'm forty-five and getting older.
After seeing the bleeding keep happening every time we have sex, I searched my symptoms online and read that it could be cervical cancer, which has terrified me.
I want an exam and a biopsy done today to find out what is wrong, and if it is cancer, I need a clear explanation of what stage it is and the treatment plan.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions that I know of, though I haven't had regular medical checkups for twelve years.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital stays other than when I delivered my two children.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter pain medications, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I smoke about one pack of cigarettes every day, and I have smoked for twenty years.
I only drink an occasional beer on weekends, maybe one or two drinks a month at most.
I work full-time as a cashier at a grocery store, and I live in an apartment with my partner.
My mother had high blood pressure and my father died of a stroke, but no one in my family had cervical, uterine, or ovarian cancer.
My last regular period started about three weeks ago, and there is no possibility that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 130/82 mmHg, heart rate is 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and body temperature is 36.8°C.
Patient appears alert, moderately anxious, and slightly fatigued, but is in no acute cardiopulmonary distress.
Palpebral conjunctivae show slight pallor, and sclerae are white without icterus.
Thyroid gland is symmetrical, non-enlarged, and non-tender without palpable nodules or bruits.
Skin is warm and dry without acne, hirsutism, or acanthosis nigricans.
Abdomen is flat and soft with mild deep tenderness on palpation over the right lower quadrant and suprapubic area, but no guarding, rebound tenderness, or palpable masses.

Speculum inspection reveals a 3.5 cm exophytic cauliflower-like friable ulcerated mass on the anterior cervical lip that bleeds easily on contact, and bimanual exam demonstrates nodular induration extending into the upper vagina and right parametrium.
Rectovaginal examination confirms right parametrial nodular thickening that does not extend to the pelvic sidewall, with smooth, intact rectal mucosa.
Mild non-pitting fullness is noted over the right lower leg without bilateral pitting edema or calf erythema.
